briefing: Brent crude settled at $113.17 a barrel Thursday, its highest close since May, after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and disputed Iranian tanker claims, keeping Ontario fuel prices high. Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford sparred over housing, taxes and Toronto Water in the last debate before Monday's tied mayoral vote. Markets still lean toward a Bank of Canada rate hike next Wednesday, a risk for variable-rate borrowers.
headline: Chow and Bradford clash in final debate; Brent settles above $113

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, 2026, in the middle of nuclear talks. The first wave killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran answered with missiles and drones on Israel, Gulf states and U.S. bases, and closed the Strait of Hormuz, the channel that roughly a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through. A peace memorandum signed in June briefly reopened shipping, but it fell apart in July when Iran started attacking commercial ships again to press its claim over the strait.
stories.headline: Brent settles at $113 as Trump calls Iran's tanker claims fake
stories.impact: This is a big part of why gas and diesel in Ontario stay expensive: GTA regular is forecast around $1.80 a litre on Friday and diesel near $2.65. Diesel feeds straight into grocery and delivery prices, and higher fuel is one reason the Bank of Canada has been cautious about cutting rates.
stories.now: Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) says four ships were hit and three more struck mines near the Strait of Hormuz; Trump said on Truth Social that Iran was making up the hits to drive up oil prices before the election, and none of the claims have been independently verified. Brent for December delivery settled up 4.0% at $113.17 a barrel and U.S. crude (WTI) rose 2.4% to $99.47 after Yemen's Houthis claimed four attacks on Saudi targets in 48 hours. Bloomberg reports Asian refiners have cut November orders of U.S. crude by about half, to roughly 24–26 million barrels, as shipping costs from the Gulf Coast to Asia have climbed to $30–35 a barrel. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) says its 100-day blockade of Iranian ports has stopped about $25 billion in Iranian crude exports, and the U.S. has ordered non-emergency staff and families out of Saudi Arabia. The New York Times reports U.S. and Israeli plans for new strikes on Iran after the midterms.

stories.why: This is the single biggest driver of global energy prices this year. Washington and Tehran are now openly disputing basic facts about attacks, and reported post-midterm strike plans suggest the conflict could widen in November.

stories.backstory: Oil prices jumped after the U.S.-Iran war closed much of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, and fuel costs have fed through to inflation since. Brent fell to about $74 in late June when shipping recovered, then climbed again as attacks resumed this autumn. Canada's central bank has weighed whether an energy-driven spike is temporary or will spread to other prices.
stories.headline: Markets bet on a Bank of Canada hike after 3.1% inflation
stories.impact: Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit would cost more within days of a hike, and anyone renewing a GTA mortgage this fall should test their budget at a higher rate. High pump prices will keep squeezing commuters either way.
stories.now: Statistics Canada says prices rose 3.1% in the year to September, up from 3.0%, just under the 3.2% economists expected; excluding gasoline, inflation slowed to 2.2%. The Bank of Canada's preferred core measures averaged 1.9%, and grocery inflation cooled to 1.7%. After the report, overnight swaps priced about an 87% chance of a quarter-point hike to 2.50% next Wednesday, up from roughly 70% earlier that day. BMO, RBC and Desjardins switched to calling for a hike and Scotiabank firmed up its call, though a Bloomberg survey of economists still leaned toward a hold. The Canadian dollar traded near 71.2 U.S. cents (about C$1.405 per U.S. dollar) Wednesday, close to a four-week high on the hike bets.

stories.backstory: Chow won a 2023 by-election after John Tory resigned and is now seeking a full term. Bradford, a councillor, is her main challenger. Late-summer polls had Chow around 50% and Bradford near 39%. Big themes are housing costs, traffic, property taxes and the province's moves on bike lanes.
stories.headline: Chow and Bradford spar over housing, taxes and water in final debate
stories.impact: You get a vote for mayor, ward councillor and school trustee in your own city. Check your municipality's site for your polling station and advance-voting hours.
stories.now: Bradford said only about 1,500 of Chow's promised 65,000 purpose-built rental homes by 2030 have been delivered; Chow answered that approvals are 80% faster and development charges are lower, and that no affordable housing was built while Bradford chaired the planning committee. Bradford called for an outside line-by-line review of the roughly $19-billion city budget and said property taxes rose nearly 20% over three years; Chow said his promised tax freeze would really work out to a 1.5% increase. On his plan to make Toronto Water an independent public utility like Toronto Hydro, Chow warned it would open the door to privatization under Premier Ford, and Bradford said provincial law bars that and pledged to resign if it happened. Before the debate, a Nanos survey for CP24 and CTV found 13% of voters open to changing their vote and 16% somewhat open, and recent Mainstreet and Pollara polls range from a near tie to a seven-point Chow lead.

stories.backstory: The U.S. has put 50% tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum and, in August, on billions of dollars of other Canadian goods, and Canada has answered with counter-tariffs. Ford has pressed Ottawa for relief for steel, auto, forestry and copper before any deal with Washington, and in August urged Carney to hold out rather than accept a bad deal.
stories.headline: Carney and Ford launch $8.7B plan for steel, autos and Ring of Fire roads
stories.impact: If you work in steel, auto parts or at an assembly plant in Hamilton, Oshawa, Windsor or the GTA, this money is meant to keep plants running and retool them. The emissions freeze could also ease pressure on automakers to raise prices on gas-powered vehicles over the next few years.
stories.now: The package puts $5 billion toward upgrading Ontario steel mills, $2.5 billion toward helping the auto sector move to electric-vehicle production and $1 billion toward roads into the Ring of Fire mineral region in Northern Ontario. Ontario's share is $2.67 billion. The two governments are also creating a Joint Steel Action Fund for steel products Canadian companies need, and Ottawa is tightening border enforcement against cheap foreign steel being dumped in Canada; the country imports more than 6.5 million tonnes of steel a year. Ottawa also froze its fleet-average emissions standard for new cars and light trucks through 2029, giving automakers short-term breathing room. Carney said the plan could create 70,000 jobs tied to the Ring of Fire and protect about 220,000 others, and Ford called it historic, saying the relationship with the U.S. has changed for good whatever happens in the midterms.

stories.summary: Ottawa and Ontario announced $8.7 billion, including $2.67 billion from the province, to modernize steel mills, help automakers shift to electric vehicles and build roads to the Ring of Fire mining region.

stories.why: It is the first big joint federal-provincial answer to the job losses U.S. tariffs have caused in Ontario's factories, and it shifts the focus from shielding old jobs to rebuilding steel and auto production for a less U.S.-dependent future.

stories.backstory: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump's broad emergency tariffs in February, but sector tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos, copper and lumber stayed. At the first CUSMA review on July 1, the U.S. refused to extend the deal for a full new term, so it now needs annual reviews. Ottawa walked out of talks on August 21, calling Washington's last-minute demands unfair. The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on August 22, and Canada matched with counter-tariffs on September 8, plus a $25B support package for affected workers and businesses.
stories.headline: Carney and Trump talk trade as U.S. embassy alleges midterm meddling
stories.impact: Tariffs raise prices on some U.S. goods in Canadian stores and squeeze manufacturing jobs in the GTA, Windsor and Hamilton. If you or your family work in autos, steel, logistics or anything that ships to the U.S., this is the story most likely to touch your paycheque.
stories.now: Carney gave few details of the call beyond saying it covered trade issues; no deal is expected before the November 3 midterms, according to CBC sources. The embassy's list quotes Industry Minister Joly five times, mostly on pressuring U.S. businesses and aiming counter-tariffs at particular states, and also quotes Ford; Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said Washington is watching for election interference. Carney replied that the U.S. started the trade actions and Canada's responses protect Canadian workers, and Ford said he has no interest in U.S. elections. A Canada-EU summit on October 29–30 is expected to deepen ties on critical minerals and defence.

stories.backstory: Russia's full-scale invasion is in its fifth year. Trump's envoys have made several trips to Moscow, while Zelenskyy has pushed for a leaders' meeting that Russia rejects. Russia has been pounding Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter, and Kyiv has struck Russian refineries in return. Ukraine has also complained about U.S. limits on intelligence sharing and a Starlink slowdown.
stories.headline: Russia used cluster warheads in Kyiv barrage, Zelenskyy says
stories.impact: Canada is a major Ukraine backer and is being asked for more money at the October 29–30 Canada-EU summit, which affects federal spending. Any real progress toward peace could ease diesel and gas prices over time.
stories.now: Zelenskyy said at least two people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, and that Russia has carried out more than 170 strikes on energy facilities since October 11. A Ukrainian adviser identified one weapon as an Iskander missile with a cluster warhead that scatters 58 bomblets over an area roughly 400 metres square. Russia also launched 210 drones, 181 of which were shot down or jammed, and hits were recorded at 32 locations. Moscow says it downed more than 800 Ukrainian drones overnight. The Kremlin says Putin agreed after a three-hour meeting with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff to resume talks with Washington and Kyiv after November 10, but Zelenskyy says the strikes show no real Russian intent to end the war.

stories.summary: Zelenskyy says three of the 21 ballistic missiles Russia fired at Kyiv overnight carried cluster warheads, one landing near the historic Pechersk Lavra monastery. The attack came hours after Putin agreed in principle to restart three-way talks after November 10.

stories.why: It is the first concrete sign in weeks that direct talks could restart, but both sides are still escalating strikes, and Moscow continues to demand all of Donetsk and no NATO membership for Kyiv. Moscow's offer to help on Iran also links the two wars driving energy prices.

stories.backstory: Republicans have controlled both the House and Senate since January 2025, which has let Trump pass his agenda with few checks. Midterms usually go against the president's party, and Trump's approval is lower than at the same point in his first term. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot. A Democratic House could launch investigations and block spending and trade legislation.
stories.headline: Supreme Court rulings reshape midterm map as Democrats sue over election moves
stories.impact: A change in Congress could shift the odds of tariff relief for Ontario's auto, steel and lumber industries. Ottawa's trade strategy is partly being timed around the outcome.
stories.now: Reuters tallies the Court's 2026 election rulings: in April it weakened a key part of the 1965 Voting Rights Act, which let several Southern states redraw districts with large Black populations; in June it struck down limits on coordinated party spending; and this month it let parties get discounted broadcast ad rates. Other rulings went against Republicans, including upholding mail-ballot grace periods and blocking Missouri's redrawn map. Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries have sued over federal voter-roll reviews, and a judge has blocked most Department of Homeland Security (DHS) voter-fraud field work in nine states. AP counts more than 13 million early votes, versus about 9 million at this point in 2022, and a New York Times/Siena poll has Democrats ahead 52% to 41% for the House. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in each chamber to take control.

stories.summary: A string of Supreme Court decisions this year on voting rights, maps and party spending is shaping the November 3 battle for Congress, as Democratic leaders sue the Trump administration over its federal election reviews and early voting runs far ahead of 2022.

stories.why: The result decides how freely Trump can act on tariffs, the Iran war and spending for the final two years of his term.

stories.backstory: Ottawa moved its budget to the fall last year so it lines up with the construction season and avoids a separate fall update. The 2025 fall budget focused on big infrastructure, housing and defence investment and ran a large deficit. Since then, 50% U.S. tariffs and Canada's counter-tariffs have hit manufacturing, and Ottawa has rolled out support packages, including $25 billion for affected workers and businesses and the new $8.7 billion plan with Ontario. The Liberals do not hold a majority, so the budget needs support from at least one other party to pass.
stories.headline: Ottawa will table its 2026 budget on November 5
stories.impact: Watch for changes to personal taxes, housing programs, EI and tariff relief for Ontario workers. Bigger deficits can also keep longer-term borrowing costs, including fixed mortgage rates, higher.
stories.now: Champagne announced the date during question period on Tuesday, saying the plan will focus on unlocking investment and creating well-paid jobs. Prime Minister Mark Carney says Ottawa is on track to balance its day-to-day operating budget in 2027-28, a year early, but the Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO) projects that target will slip by a year. The PBO also expects the overall deficit to stay above $63 billion later this decade rather than falling to the $53 billion the government projected. Defence spending is set to rise from about $75 billion a year to $95.7 billion by 2030-31. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has attacked the government's spending plans.

stories.backstory: Cleveland-Cliffs, an Ohio steelmaker, bought Hamilton-based Stelco in 2024, and Ottawa approved the deal on condition that union jobs and most non-union roles be kept. U.S. 50% tariffs on Canadian steel since August have hit exports hard. In early October Stelco announced a partial shutdown of finishing lines at Hamilton Works, cutting up to 500 jobs, and Joly gave the company five days to respond. The dispute has become a test of whether Ottawa can enforce foreign-takeover promises.
stories.headline: Ford backs Ottawa's fight with Stelco over 500 Hamilton layoffs
stories.impact: Hundreds of Hamilton families face lost paycheques, with knock-on effects for suppliers and the local economy. The outcome may shape whether the new federal-Ontario steel fund keeps similar plants running.
stories.now: Ford said a company should not walk away from its commitments and promised to work with Ottawa to protect Stelco workers and steelworkers across Ontario. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has warned Cleveland-Cliffs it could face penalties or a court-ordered sale of its Canadian assets if it does not keep the jobs it promised under the Investment Canada Act. Stelco says it remains in compliance and that its 2024 undertakings do not bar layoffs, blaming 50% U.S. tariffs for a steep drop in U.S. sales. Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves has accused Ottawa of bullying, while Carney says the company betrayed workers and that money is available to keep them on the job.

stories.backstory: In spring 2023, about 155,000 federal workers struck for almost two weeks, one of the largest strikes in Canadian history, before winning raises totalling 12.6% over four years. Since then Ottawa has ordered public servants back to the office more days a week and is cutting its workforce to control spending. The federal budget is due November 5.
stories.headline: 120,000 federal workers to hold strike votes
stories.impact: No strike can happen before voting ends in January, so services are normal for now. If you need a passport or federal benefit paperwork early next year, consider applying sooner.
stories.now: The workers include passport and benefits officers, wildland firefighters, fishery officers, federal teachers, librarians and administrative staff. PSAC says Treasury Board, the federal employer, will not bargain on wages, job security, remote work or protection from artificial intelligence (AI) replacing jobs. Talks have dragged on for about a year and a half, and in May the union called a wage offer below 1% a year insulting. The government has not publicly responded to the vote announcement.

stories.summary: The Public Service Alliance of Canada (PSAC), the biggest federal public-service union, will hold strike votes for about 120,000 workers from November 16 to January 22 after talks with the government broke down.

stories.why: A strike would hit services Canadians use directly, from passports to benefit payments. It also tests how hard Ottawa will hold the line on spending ahead of the budget.

stories.backstory: Ontario's housing market has been sluggish for more than two years, with condo sales in the GTA especially weak and builders cutting new projects. Higher inflation this fall, driven by gas prices, has shifted talk from rate cuts to possible hikes.
stories.headline: GTA new condo sales hit a September record low
stories.impact: Buyers of new low-rise homes have more bargaining power and lower prices than a year ago, and condo builders are under pressure to discount. Anyone renewing a mortgage should plan for rates that could rise rather than fall.
stories.now: BILD, using Altus Group data, says 949 new homes sold in September, 52% below the 10-year average; high-rise sales fell 40% from a year earlier and were 90% below normal, while 820 low-rise sales ran 17% above average. The benchmark price for new low-rise homes fell 13.3% over the year to about $1.25 million, while new condos held flat near $1.03 million. Unsold condo inventory stands at about 12,900 units, roughly 49 months of supply. On Wednesday, Desjardins forecast Ontario resale activity up almost 5% and prices up 2.4% in 2027, but warned expected Bank of Canada hikes could cap the rebound.

sources.title: BILD (GlobeNewswire): GTA new high-rise sales hit record low

stories.summary: Only 129 new high-rise homes sold in the GTA in September, a record low for the month, even as low-rise sales beat their 10-year average, according to the Building Industry and Land Development Association (BILD).

timeline.event: Housing starts peak in Ontario.

stories.why: The collapse in new condo sales means fewer projects break ground, which could tighten supply and push rents and prices up again later in the decade.

stories.backstory: Since the U.S. trade war began, Ottawa has been trying to sell more to countries other than the U.S., with a goal of doubling non-U.S. exports within a decade. Carney attended the NATO summit in Ankara in July. Canada lifted some export restrictions on Türkiye in 2024 after years of tension over drone parts. Türkiye is a NATO ally with a large defence and aerospace industry.
stories.headline: Carney and Erdogan launch Canada-Türkiye partnership and free trade talks
stories.impact: Little immediate change for GTA households. Ontario aerospace, nuclear-supply and mining firms could gain new customers if talks progress.
stories.now: The partnership comes with a three-year action plan built on four areas: trade and investment, defence and security, energy, and ties between people. Two-way trade is about $3 billion; Erdogan said the goal is $5 billion first and eventually $10 billion, with a first round of trade talks in Ankara next month. Energy ministers will work on liquefied natural gas (LNG), nuclear power and critical minerals, and Türkiye is weighing Canadian nuclear technology. Carney said the aim is collective resilience rather than self-sufficiency. Some Armenian-Canadians voiced alarm about the trip, which also comes amid a Turkish crackdown on LGBTQ+ people.

stories.why: It is part of Ottawa's push to reduce reliance on the U.S. market while 50% U.S. tariffs bite. A trade deal would take years, so the near-term effect is modest.

stories.backstory: A June Supreme Court ruling struck down limits on how much parties can coordinate spending with candidates, opening the door to larger late campaigns. Republicans are defending slim majorities in both chambers amid Trump's low approval ratings, high living costs and the unpopular Iran war. Republicans hold a large fundraising edge, helped by billionaire donors including Elon Musk.
stories.headline: Trump groups spend $277M in late midterm blitz; pollster admits fake data
stories.impact: Mostly a U.S. story, but it shapes who sets tariff policy toward Canada after November 3. Treat single polls with caution, including in Toronto's own tight race.
stories.now: Federal filings show MAGA Inc. did most of the spending, including $200 million sent to No Going Back PAC and $25 million to Safety & Affordability PAC; it had about $164 million left on October 14 after starting September with nearly $416 million. Trump says he will spend more than $400 million by Election Day, and Texas's Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico is a major target. Separately, Wedgewood Polling admitted on October 20 that the vast majority of its data was made up, calling it an experiment to expose industry weaknesses; outlets including the New York Times removed its polls from their averages. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) chair Brendan Carr warned broadcasters that airing fake polls could breach their obligations.

stories.summary: Trump's political groups have spent nearly $277 million since early September to help Republicans, new filings show, while a national pollster admitted most of its published polls were fabricated.

stories.backstory: In February the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump's broad tariffs that relied on an emergency-powers law (IEEPA). The administration then turned to other laws, and in August imposed 50% tariffs on many Canadian goods after trade talks broke down. The Liberty Justice Center also helped bring one of the earlier cases that went to the Supreme Court.
stories.headline: U.S. importer sues to strike down Trump's 50% tariffs on Canada
stories.impact: A win would lower costs for Ontario exporters selling into the U.S. and could ease pressure on GTA manufacturing jobs, but nothing changes for now.
stories.now: The suit, filed Tuesday by the Liberty Justice Center on behalf of Gellert and a proposed class of importers, argues the administration went beyond its powers under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a rarely used law that lets a president respond to foreign trade discrimination. Gellert imports Canadian food products such as cheese. It asks the court to stop the duties and order refunds with interest. The White House has not yet filed a response.

stories.summary: New Jersey food importer Gellert Global Group has asked the U.S. Court of International Trade to block Trump's 50% tariffs on Canadian goods and refund what importers paid.

timeline.event: Supreme Court strikes down emergency (IEEPA) tariffs.
U.S. 50% tariffs on Canadian goods take effect.
Gellert sues at the Court of International Trade.

stories.why: If the court agrees, it would be the second time a U.S. court has knocked out Trump's tariffs on Canada, and importers could be owed refunds. A ruling is likely months away.
